title: What training does an OSHA emergency action plan require?
description: OSHA 1910.38(e) and (f) emergency action plan training and plan review, plus 1910.39 fire prevention plan information duties, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Under the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standard 29 CFR 1910.38, an employer must designate and train employees to assist in a safe and orderly evacuation, and review the emergency action plan with each covered employee when the plan is developed or the employee is first assigned, when their responsibilities change, and when the plan changes. The companion fire prevention plan standard, 29 CFR 1910.39, requires employees to be told of the fire hazards they face on initial assignment.
keyTakeaways: Section 1910.38 applies whenever another OSHA standard in part 1910 requires an emergency action plan, for example 1910.157 for portable fire extinguishers and 1910.119 for process safety management.
Paragraph (e) requires the employer to designate and train employees to assist in evacuation, which is a role-based training duty.
Paragraph (f) requires plan review with each covered employee at three trigger points, not on a fixed annual cycle.
Section 1910.39(d) requires employees to be informed of their fire hazards on initial assignment and to have the self-protection parts of the fire prevention plan reviewed with them.
Employers with 10 or fewer employees may communicate both plans orally under 1910.38(b) and 1910.39(b).
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: General industry employers required by an OSHA standard in part 1910 to have an emergency action plan or fire prevention plan
All employees covered by the plan
Employees designated to assist in evacuation, such as floor wardens and sweepers
Employees who remain to operate critical plant operations or perform rescue or medical duties

sections.heading: When is an emergency action plan required?

blocks.text: An emergency action plan is required whenever an OSHA standard in part 1910 requires one. Paragraph (a) of [29 CFR 1910.38](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.38) is a scope provision: the section does not itself require a plan, it sets the content for every plan that another standard requires. The same structure applies to fire prevention plans under paragraph (a) of [29 CFR 1910.39](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.39).

OSHA's [Evacuation Plans and Procedures eTool questionnaire](https://www.osha.gov/etools/evacuation-plans-procedures/expert-systems/osha-requirements) lists the common triggers: fire extinguishers provided in the workplace, certain total flooding extinguishing systems, fire detection systems with alarms delayed by more than 30 seconds, and compliance duties under process safety management (1910.119), grain handling facilities (1910.272), ethylene oxide (1910.1047), methylenedianiline (1910.1050) and 1,3-butadiene (1910.1051). The questionnaire also notes that employers whose own employees will respond to a hazardous substance release need an emergency response plan under 1910.120(q) instead.

sections.heading: Who must be trained under paragraph (e)?

blocks.text: Paragraph (e) requires the employer to "designate and train employees to assist in a safe and orderly evacuation of other employees." It is a duty to create a trained role, not a duty to train everyone in the same way. The standard does not set a number, a curriculum or an interval for these employees.

OSHA's eTool page on [developing and implementing an emergency action plan](https://www.osha.gov/etools/evacuation-plans-procedures/eap/develop-implement) reads paragraph (e) as requiring the employer to "designate and train enough people" before implementing the plan. The same page recommends, without making it mandatory, that effective plans call for retraining employees annually and include evacuation drills. That distinction matters for audit: an annual cycle is good practice, while the regulatory duty is to have trained designees in place.

The content of designee training follows from the minimum plan elements in paragraph (c): procedures for reporting a fire or other emergency, evacuation procedures and exit route assignments, procedures for employees who remain to operate critical plant operations before they evacuate, procedures to account for all employees after evacuation, procedures for employees performing rescue or medical duties, and the name or job title of every contact for questions about the plan.

sections.heading: When must the plan be reviewed with each employee?

blocks.text: Paragraph (f) requires review with each covered employee at three points, and only at those points. They are listed below with the practical event that usually signals each one.

blocks.text: Paragraph (b) requires the plan to be in writing, kept in the workplace and available to employees for review, except that an employer with 10 or fewer employees may communicate it orally. Paragraph (d) requires an employee alarm system that uses a distinctive signal for each purpose and complies with 1910.165, which is itself content employees need to recognize.

sections.heading: What does the fire prevention plan add?

blocks.text: Section 1910.39 adds an information duty rather than a training program. Under paragraph (d), the employer must inform employees upon initial assignment to a job of the fire hazards to which they are exposed, and must review with each employee those parts of the fire prevention plan necessary for self-protection.

The plan content in paragraph (c) defines what that review draws from: a list of all major fire hazards, proper handling and storage of hazardous materials, potential ignition sources and their control, and the fire protection equipment needed for each major hazard; procedures to control accumulations of flammable and combustible waste; procedures for maintaining safeguards on heat-producing equipment; and the name or job title of employees responsible for maintaining ignition control equipment and for controlling fuel source hazards. Those named employees need deeper training than the general workforce, because the plan assigns them specific duties.

sections.heading: What evidence shows emergency plan training is compliant?

blocks.text: Neither section prescribes a training record, so evidence has to be designed. The table maps each duty to the people it applies to, its trigger, and what an inspector or auditor would reasonably expect to see.

sections.heading: How should employers structure emergency plan training?

blocks.text: Treat the plan as a controlled document and the review as a version acknowledgment. Because paragraph (f)(3) is triggered by any plan change, the plan's revision history is the driver for retraining, and each revision should identify which employees need a review. Designee training can then sit on an annual cycle as recommended practice, with drills providing observed evidence.

Where portable fire extinguishers are provided for employee use, the emergency action plan also defines who is designated to fight fires, and those employees need annual training under 1910.157(g)(3) and (g)(4); see [OSHA fire extinguisher training requirements](/regulations/osha-fire-extinguisher-training-requirements). Process safety sites should read this page alongside [OSHA process safety management training](/regulations/osha-process-safety-management-training-requirements). For the overview of OSHA duties, see [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements), and for managing plan revisions as controlled documents see [how to maintain version control for training content](/guides/how-to-maintain-version-control-for-training-content).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each plan element in 1910.38(c) to the roles that act on it, so a revision to one element identifies the employees whose review is triggered under paragraph (f)(3). Designated roles are tracked separately from the general review, because paragraph (e) is a training duty and paragraph (f) is a review duty.

faqs.q: Does OSHA require annual emergency action plan training?
faqs.a: No fixed interval is set in 1910.38. Paragraph (f) requires review at initial assignment or plan development, when responsibilities change, and when the plan changes. OSHA's eTool recommends annual retraining and drills as features of effective plans, but describes them as practices rather than requirements.

faqs.q: Can a small business deliver its emergency action plan orally?
faqs.a: Yes. Under 1910.38(b), an employer with 10 or fewer employees may communicate the plan orally. Section 1910.39(b) allows the same for fire prevention plans. The review triggers in 1910.38(f) still apply, so an oral plan should still be reviewed at each trigger.

faqs.q: Is an emergency action plan the same as an emergency response plan?
faqs.a: No. An emergency action plan under 1910.38 covers evacuation and related actions. Where employees will respond to a hazardous substance release themselves, OSHA's eTool points to an emergency response plan under 1910.120(q), which carries its own training requirements; see the HAZWOPER page for those.

faqs.q: Do evacuation drills count as training?
faqs.a: A drill can be evidence that designated employees can carry out their role and that employees know their exit routes. The standard does not require drills, so they supplement rather than replace the review in paragraph (f) and the designee training in paragraph (e).

factCheck.claim: 1910.38(a): EAP required whenever an OSHA standard in this part requires one; (b) written, kept in workplace, available; 10 or fewer employees may communicate orally.
1910.38(c)(1)-(6) minimum elements; (d) employee alarm system with distinctive signal per purpose, complying with 1910.165.

1910.38(e): designate and train employees to assist in safe and orderly evacuation; (f)(1)-(3) review plan with each employee at development or initial assignment, when responsibilities change, when plan changes.

1910.39(a)-(d): FPP when a standard requires one; written or oral for 10 or fewer; minimum elements (c)(1)-(5); (d) inform employees of fire hazards on initial assignment and review self-protection parts.

OSHA eTool questionnaire lists EAP triggers: extinguishers, total flooding systems, fire detection alarms delayed over 30 seconds, 1910.119, 1910.272, 1910.1047, 1910.1050, 1910.1051; points to 1910.120(q) for employee response.
OSHA eTool: designate and train enough people per 1910.38(e); effective plans often call for retraining annually and drills (recommendation, not requirement).
